content.body:
My best friend's mother died from complications of chronic constipation.

She had been dealing with it for years.

Nobody tells us this can happen.

Helen was 74. She had lived in an assisted living facility for the last three years of her life. The staff kept calling her constipation "a normal part of aging." So did her doctor.

And it hurts me to admit this.

But so did I. Her daughter's best friend since seventh grade, and I said the same thing everyone else said. "She'll be fine. It's common at her age."

Helen had been on MiraLAX daily for eleven years. When that stopped working, they added Dulcolax. When that stopped, they gave her a prescription her daughter Vera could never remember the name of. The doses kept going up. The intervals between movements kept getting longer.

Nobody in that facility ever asked why it was getting worse. They treated each episode as a separate problem and moved on to the next one.

Then one Tuesday, Helen did not respond when the nurse came in for morning vitals.

She had been impacted for days. Nobody had documented it. The impaction had caused a bowel perforation. By the time they got her to the hospital, the infection had already spread through her abdomen.

Sepsis. She lasted four days in the ICU.

Vera called me from the hospital parking lot at midnight. I could barely understand her through the crying.

I held her hand in the hallway outside the ICU at 4 AM on a Thursday while the monitors beeped and neither of us said anything.

Helen died that morning.

...

Then two years later, four years into my own menopause, my bowels started going the same direction.

And nobody in my life, including me, connected it to what had happened to Helen.

...

I was 52 and I had been taking MiraLAX every morning for the past year and a half.

My GI doctor called it normal. "Common for women our age. We manage it."

I believed her. Because Helen's doctor had said the same thing. And because I was still carrying the weight of watching my best friend lose her mother and I did not have the energy to push back on a doctor telling me not to worry.

Then last March, on the third week of a MiraLAX dose that had already been doubled, I started feeling off.

I had not gone in eight days. The cramping started on a Friday night. A dull constant pressure low in my abdomen that would not let up. My husband asked me if I wanted to go to urgent care and I waved him off because I had been through this cycle too many times to count.

Take the extra dose. Drink the water. Wait it out. That was the drill.

But by Sunday night the pain had shifted. Sharper. Deeper. I was sweating and shivering at the same time. I could not sit still and I could not lie down.

He put me in the car and drove me to the ER whether I wanted to go or not.

The CT showed fecal loading throughout my colon. Thinned walls. The ER doctor used the word "perforation risk" and called in a surgical consult.

The surgeon came in at 6 AM. She read the scan. She looked at me.

"If this happens again, we are talking about a colostomy."

Twelve hours from the same thing that killed Helen.

I spent three days in that hospital bed thinking about her.

About the phone calls from the facility that Vera had mentioned in passing. "Mom's backed up again, they're adjusting her dose." How many times had I heard that and said nothing? How many times had Vera told me about another medication change and I had nodded and moved on?

Helen had been on laxatives almost constantly for the last five years of her life.

I had assumed, like everyone around her, that this was what happened to women her age.

But lying in that hospital bed two years later, twenty-two years younger than Helen had been when she died, I realized we had all been wrong. The constipation was not random. It was not aging in the way we had been told. It was a symptom of something nobody had ever looked into.

And nobody was looking into mine either.

Six weeks after I was discharged, I found a doctor one town over who came recommended through a friend at church.

I booked the appointment because twelve hours from emergency surgery had a way of clarifying what was worth a co-pay.

Also because I kept seeing Helen's face in that hospital bed.

And I did not want Vera holding my hand the same way I had held hers.

Dr. Vogel was different from the start.

She did not look at her computer for the first fifteen minutes. She listened to me tell the whole story. The MiraLAX. The ER. The surgical consult. Helen.

When I finished, she did not reach for her prescription pad.

She pulled out a marker and drew three overlapping circles on the exam table paper.

"Your constipation is not random," she said quietly.

"Your colon stopped being able to move waste on its own years ago. And Helen's probably stopped a decade before that."

She called it the Slick Layer Collapse.

"Your colon moves waste along a thin, slick coating on the inside wall. Think of it like the coating on a factory conveyor belt. When the coating is intact, everything slides along. When the coating wears through, product piles up on the belt no matter how fast you run the motor."

She pointed to the first circle.

"The coating, your mucus layer, has thinned."

She pointed to the second.

"The bacteria that lived in that coating are gone. They are the ones that produce a compound called butyrate. Butyrate is the signal that tells your colon to squeeze."

She pointed to the third.

"The signal itself has gone quiet. Your colon is not broken. It has not forgotten how to work. It is waiting for a message that is no longer being sent."

She circled where all three overlapped.

"This is where you are living now. And laxatives do not fix any of it. They make it worse."

I asked her what she meant.

"MiraLAX pulls water into the pipe. That water washes through the mucus layer, thinning it further. It also flushes out the bacteria that were trying to hold on. Each scoop of MiraLAX strips a little more of the coating and a few more of the bacteria. Which is why your next bad spell comes sooner than the last one. And the one after that is worse. And so on, until something that used to be manageable nearly puts you on an operating table."

I thought about the eleven years of daily MiraLAX before Helen died.

Each scoop making the next episode more likely.

She had been in a cycle nobody was trying to stop.

I asked what had caused the coating to thin in the first place.

"This is the part that is hard to hear," she said. "Researchers found that in animal studies, oral exposure to polystyrene microplastics caused constipation directly. Decreased motility. Thinned mucus layers. Suppressed the genes that build the coating in the first place."

She paused.

"You know those plastic containers we've all been microwaving leftovers in for thirty years? Nobody did anything wrong. Everyone was living the same way."

"Nobody has proven this happens in your colon specifically. What has been proven is that your colon looks exactly like a colon that this happened to."

"So what actually fixes it?" I asked.

She leaned back.

"Rebuilding all three systems at once. The coating. The bacteria. The signal. You cannot fix one without fixing the others. Most women never break the cycle because they address one piece at a time. MiraLAX for the movement. A probiotic for the bacteria. Fiber for the bulk. None of them work alone because the housing for the bacteria does not exist anymore."

She wrote on her notepad.

"Black elderberry anthocyanins. Cold-extracted, never heated. The anthocyanins are the specific food that the butyrate-producing bacteria eat. When you feed them, they expand. When they expand, butyrate production restarts. The signal comes back."

"Zinc citrate for lining repair. Buffered vitamin C to support the mucosal barrier."

"Find something that has all three together. Not separately. The gummies at the drugstore are heat-processed and the anthocyanins are destroyed before they reach your gut."

I went home that night and opened my laptop.

Most supplements had one ingredient. Maybe two. The elderberry products were all gummies, cooked at high heat, with a fraction of the dose. The probiotics were generic strains with nothing to do with the mucus layer. Nothing combined all three.

I was about to give up when I found a Reddit thread about chronic constipation that had over 600 comments.

And halfway down the thread, a group of women were talking about the same thing.

One name kept coming up. A cold-extracted elderberry product that had the full clinical dose. One woman said she had been on MiraLAX for nine years and went on her own for the first time in week two. Another said her days-between went from six to one in a month. I kept scrolling and the same name kept appearing.

Elvera.

So I pulled up the ingredient panel.

Cold-extracted heirloom elderberry. Full clinical dose of anthocyanins. The exact compound Dr. Vogel had named.

Zinc citrate. Buffered vitamin C. Exactly what she had written down.

Everything she told me to find was in one capsule.

I sat there and did the math on what the last four years had cost me.

Eighteen months of MiraLAX at $26 a month. A year of Linzess at $45 a month with insurance. Four GI appointments at $180 each. The ER visit and three-day admission: $11,400 after insurance.

Over $13,000 treating a symptom nobody ever explained the cause of.

Elvera was $67.20 for three bottles.

I placed the order from my kitchen table at 10 PM on a Tuesday.

Day three. I noticed the constant low bloat I had been carrying as background noise for three years had started to ease. My abdomen felt quieter.

Day eight. I had a bowel movement without MiraLAX for the first time in over a year. It was not dramatic. I went to the bathroom in the morning and it happened. I stood there afterward and did not know what to do with myself.

Day fourteen. The point where my next bad spell should have arrived based on the old schedule.

Nothing happened.

I went on my own that morning. For the first time in I do not remember how long.

Day twenty-one. I slept through the night without the cramping that used to wake me at 3 AM.

Day forty-two. Another mark where a bad episode should have come. Still nothing. Still going every morning. On my own.

I went back to Dr. Vogel eight weeks later.

She ran a stool panel and looked up with a small nod.

"Your butyrate is 21.3. That is well within normal range. And your Akkermansia levels are higher than I would expect for someone who was undetectable two months ago."

I pulled the Elvera bottle out of my purse.

She nodded.

"That is exactly what I was hoping you would find."

Here is what I want every woman reading this to understand.

If you have been dealing with chronic constipation, you are not unlucky. You are not eating the wrong things. You are not drinking too little water.

Your colon has lost the coating it needs to move waste on its own. And every scoop of MiraLAX is making the next episode more likely, not less.

Laxatives force the movement this week. But they also strip the mucus and flush out the bacteria you have left. Which is why the next bad spell comes sooner. And the one after that is worse.

Your body needs the bacteria that produce the signal. Those bacteria need a coating to live in. And they need anthocyanins to eat. Elvera feeds them. Not with stimulants. Not with osmotic agents. With the specific food your gut bacteria need to rebuild the lining and help restore the signal on their own.

Fed, not forced.

I cannot change what happened to Helen. What I can do is address the upstream signal in my own body. And make sure the women around me know what she never got the chance to learn.

If your doctor keeps prescribing laxatives and calling chronic constipation "part of aging," they are treating the downstream symptom and ignoring the upstream cause. Helen died from that kind of care. I nearly did too.

Over 100,000 women are taking Elvera.

https://tryelvera.com

P.S. I visited Helen's grave last Sunday.

I brought the bottle of Elvera I had been taking. I do not know why exactly. It felt like she should see it.

I sat on the grass and told her what I had finally figured out. That her constipation had not been "normal." That the MiraLAX they kept giving her had made it worse, year after year, stripping the coating her bacteria needed to survive. That if we had known what was happening underneath, we could have asked different questions.

I told her I was sorry I had not asked more questions when it mattered.

Then I told her I had called Vera that morning. And my sister. And three friends from church. Everyone with a mother or a sister or a friend still taking MiraLAX every morning and being told it was fine.

"I am going to make sure nobody else's daughter has to go through what Vera went through," I said to the headstone.

Day fourteen. When the next bad spell should have come. Nothing. I went on my own that morning. For the first time in I do not remember how long.

And I finally felt like I was doing something to honor Helen instead of missing her.

Nina
